original_value: This article analyzes how the notion of “sovereignty” has been and is still mobilized in the realm of the digital. This notion is increasingly used to describe various forms of independence, control, and autonomy over digital infrastructures, technologies, and data. Our analysis originates from our previous and current research with activist “tech collectives” where we observed a use of the notion to emphasize alternative technological practices in a way that significantly differs from a governmental policy perspective. In this article, we review several publications in order to show the difference, if not diverging ways in which the notion is being conceptualized, in particular by different groups. We show that while the notion is generally used to assert some form of collective control on digital content and/or infrastructures, the precise interpretations, subjects, meanings, and definitions of sovereignty can significantly differ.

result.paraphrase: This article examines how the idea of “sovereignty” has been, and continues to be, invoked in the digital sphere. It is increasingly employed to refer to different forms of independence, control, and autonomy over digital infrastructures, technologies, and data. Drawing on our prior and ongoing research with activist “tech collectives,” we found that the term is used to highlight alternative technological practices in a manner that differs markedly from a governmental policy viewpoint. In this article, we survey several publications to illustrate the differences, or at least the divergent ways, in which the concept is framed, especially across different groups. We show that although it is generally used to claim some form of collective control over digital content and/or infrastructures, the specific interpretations, subjects, meanings, and definitions of sovereignty can vary considerably.
